historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Vitamin K antagonists

starting.description: Veterinary investigation linked a serious cattle bleeding and clotting disorder to spoiled sweet-clover hay. Link's laboratory developed the observed biological effect into an assay-guided search for the hay's active hemorrhagic factor, leading to crystalline dicumarol. Link later reported a farmer's visit as a further stimulus, but Burris questioned details of that retrospective anecdote; the founding observation does not depend on it.

inspiration.description: The inspiration was the observed hemorrhagic and impaired-coagulation effect in livestock fed spoiled sweet-clover hay, followed through bioassay to dicumarol isolated from that material. The later drug warfarin was a synthetic analogue, not a compound shown here to have been isolated from hay.

steps.description: Veterinarians linked cattle hemorrhage and impaired coagulation with spoiled sweet-clover hay; the laboratory took up the agricultural problem. Link later reported a chance 1933 farmer encounter as an additional stimulus, with details expressly questioned by Burris.

Bioassay-guided extraction led to a crystalline hemorrhagic factor, and structural work identified it as dicumarol; synthesis produced material matching the isolated product chemically and in animal effects.
By 1940, the laboratory was deliberately preparing related compounds and considering their potential medical use, seeking synthetic analogues with stronger effects than the identified lead.

Rat work published in 1942 documented that vitamin K counteracted dicumarol-induced hypoprothrombinemia, a physiological relationship relevant to the class, without resolving its molecular mechanism in that paper.
The laboratory prepared and assayed further related 4-hydroxycoumarin structures; no. 42 was selected after animal testing and developed as warfarin.
Warfarin was marketed for rodent control and later used clinically in a more water-soluble sodium form; ACS dates human-use approval to 1954.

design.description: Researchers synthesized the identified active hay compound, made structurally related 4-hydroxycoumarin analogues, compared their biological effects across animal models, selected warfarin no. 42, and developed a more water-soluble sodium form. The analogue series changes active structure and biological activity; it is not merely a delivery adjustment. These intentional contributions follow the observed hemorrhagic lead.

circumstances.description: The designation combines an observed livestock disease and Link's reported chance farmer visit with deliberate assay-guided isolation, synthesis and analogue development. Details of the retrospective visit are questioned by Burris; the chance encounter is a reported circumstance, not an independently established scene or a necessary premise of the observation-led judgment.

limits: The supported founding chain is the assigned spoiled-hay–dicumarol–warfarin 4-hydroxycoumarin lineage. The cohort member is warfarin; other vitamin K antagonist founding lineages were not investigated and should not be inferred from this record.

Dicumarol was identified in spoiled hay, but warfarin no. 42 was a later synthetic analogue. Compound no. 63 was a distinct related compound, not warfarin; it is not treated as a separate founding branch here.
The 1942 vitamin K study establishes an experimental physiological antagonism in rats; no modern molecular mechanism or causally necessary design rationale is inferred from it.
conflicts: Burris1994 p.183 explicitly questions details of Link's1959 farmer-visit narrative, citing late-recorded quotations, changes in reported journey and weather, discrepancies with original documents and recollections of early workers. The visit is retained as Link's report with this uncertainty; the livestock observations and laboratory development do not depend on its dramatic details.

Link's 1959 retrospective reports that early clinical reports denied vitamin K reversal of dicumarol's action, whereas the 1942 Overman animal experiment reports antagonism. Species and contexts differ; these sources do not by themselves adjudicate every early clinical observation.

A non-founding anecdote differs: Burris says Eisenhower received dicumarol after his heart attack, while ACS says warfarin. The treatment detail was not independently adjudicated and is not used in the origin judgment.
gaps: Final source review independently read indexed OCR with the correct 1941 title, authors and pages for Stahmann, Huebner and Link. The live PDF route redirected to a different 1944 article and the publisher PDF was blocked. The indexed 1941 text supports the stated structure/synthesis and rabbit prothrombin comparisons; it does not provide a complete multispecies dose-response report or replace the separate original isolation paper. Downloadable 1941 PDF/page images remained unavailable.
The contemporaneous original veterinary publications of Schofield and Roderick were not separately read; their observations are attributed to Link's retrospective.

The separate Campbell and Link isolation report, the 1903 chemical synthesis report cited in the reproduced letter, and Link's original 1940 letter were not separately read. The 1941 structure/synthesis paper and the text of the letter reproduced by Burris were read.
The early warfarin clinical papers and primary approval records were not separately read; establishment and the 1954 approval year are attributed to the Link and ACS retrospective accounts.

The original 1941 and 1942 papers were read through indexed or hosted full-text transcriptions; downloadable PDFs were not obtained. The ACS source was read in a web index. Source access does not establish independent verification of every passage.
